clinicalPearls: Three trypanosome species cause human disease: T. cruzi causes Chagas disease (American trypanosomiasis); T. brucei gambiense and T. b. rhodesiense cause human African trypanosomiasis (HAT, 'sleeping sickness'). Both are vector-borne neglected tropical diseases (p.1788).

Chagas is transmitted mainly by intradomiciliary triatomine ('reduviid') bugs whose feces, deposited during a nighttime blood meal, carry the infective metacyclic form that enters through skin breaks, mucosae, or conjunctivae; nonvectorial routes include congenital, blood transfusion, organ/tissue transplant, and oral (contaminated food/drink) transmission (p.1788).
Acute Chagas is asymptomatic or a mild febrile illness in >90% of cases; characteristic local swelling at the inoculation site is the Romaña sign (eyelid) or chagoma (skin) (p.1789-1790).

After acute infection T. cruzi persists for life in most patients; 60-70% remain in the indeterminate form (no apparent tissue damage), while 30-40% progress over decades to determinate disease - cardiac (20-30%), digestive (5-20%), or mixed (5-10%) (p.1789).

Chronic Chagas cardiomyopathy produces a dilated cardiomyopathy with fibrosis, segmental contractility loss, left ventricular apical aneurysm, ventricular arrhythmias, and conduction system disease; advanced cardiac damage carries a worse prognosis than other cardiomyopathies including ischemic disease (p.1789-1790).

Digestive Chagas (megaviscera) results from destruction of intramural autonomic ganglion cells: esophageal involvement mimics achalasia and colonic involvement mimics Hirschsprung's disease, with severe constipation, fecaloma, and risk of volvulus and toxic dilation; megacolon is diagnosed when sigmoid/descending colon diameter is >=6.5 cm (p.1789, 1791).

Chagas diagnosis is stage-dependent: detect circulating parasites by blood microscopy after concentration (Strout, microhematocrit) or PCR during acute phase/reactivation; rely on serology (anti-T. cruzi IgG) once parasitemia is subpatent in the chronic phase - two positive tests using different techniques and antigens confirm chronic infection (p.1790).

12-lead ECG (with 30-s strip) is a good screening test for Chagas cardiomyopathy; common abnormalities are right bundle branch block, left anterior fascicular block, ventricular premature beats, repolarization disorders, Q waves, and low QRS voltage (p.1791).

HAT is restricted to sub-Saharan Africa, matching the range of its tsetse fly (Glossina) vector; T. b. gambiense (western/central Africa, humans are main reservoir, slow chronic course) differs from T. b. rhodesiense (eastern/southeastern Africa, zoonotic animal reservoirs, acute course) (p.1792-1793).

T. b. gambiense HAT is a slowly evolving illness with a long incubation (months to years); T. b. rhodesiense HAT is an acute febrile illness with a short (<3-week) incubation and a shorter (weeks to months) course (p.1794).

A trypanosomal chancre may develop at the tsetse bite site (more common in travelers and in T. b. rhodesiense); it is nonpurulent, painful, itchy, and resolves spontaneously in 1-3 weeks (p.1794-1795).
Enlarged cervical lymph nodes are a classic HAT sign (38-85% of patients); posterior cervical involvement is the Winterbottom sign - cervical palpation is essential in suspected HAT (p.1794).

HAT is called 'sleeping sickness' because of CNS (second-stage) sleep disturbances - daytime somnolence, nocturnal insomnia, dysregulated sleep/wake cycle and fragmented sleep - plus neuropsychiatric features (mood/behavioral change, psychosis, motor/extrapyramidal/cerebellar syndromes) that may mimic primary psychiatric illness (p.1794).

HAT staging is by CSF examination: second-stage (CNS) disease is defined by CSF leukocytes >5/uL and/or trypanosomes; T. b. gambiense screening uses serology (card agglutination test, CATT, or lateral flow tests) and confirmation by microscopy of trypanosomes in lymph, blood, skin, or CSF (p.1795).

T. b. rhodesiense diagnosis is usually simpler because parasites are more numerous in blood; wet mounts, thin/thick Giemsa smears, and concentration techniques serve for both screening and confirmation, and parasites may be seen in chancre aspirate (p.1795).

T. cruzi evades immunity to persist as low-grade amastigote replication; immunosuppression (HIV, post-transplant, hematologic malignancy) can cause reactivation with increased parasitemia and CNS/cardiac/skin lesions - clinically manifest reactivation is an AIDS-defining opportunistic infection (~20% risk in untreated HIV when CD4 <100/uL) (p.1789).
harrison.pathophysiology: Chagas (T. cruzi): trypomastigotes inoculated via triatomine feces enter the bloodstream, infect nucleated cells (notably cardiac, skeletal, and smooth muscle) and differentiate into amastigotes. An innate response to parasite mucins/DNA drives a predominantly Th1 response with proinflammatory cytokines and CD8+ T-cell activation that reduces parasitemia to subpatent levels in 4-8 weeks (end of acute phase). Immune evasion permits lifelong low-intensity amastigote proliferation. Chronic damage is thought to arise from parasite persistence plus a dysregulated host immune response (Th1/Th2 imbalance, excess proinflammatory cytokines), with secondary microcirculatory abnormalities and dysautonomia; the role of autoimmune mechanisms remains unresolved. In myocardium, chronic inflammation causes cellular destruction and fibrosis, segmental loss of contractility, chamber dilation, apical aneurysm, ventricular arrhythmias, and conduction-system scarring, plus autonomic (vagal/sympathetic) denervation. In the gut, a direct toxic effect on intramural autonomic ganglion cells causes loss of neural cells, motility disorders, and organ dilation (megaviscera). African trypanosomiasis (T. b. gambiense/rhodesiense): these subspecies infect humans because they resist human serum lytic factor apolipoprotein L-1 (T. b. rhodesiense via serum resistance-associated protein; T. b. gambiense via TgsGP glycoprotein and other mechanisms). After tsetse bite and local inflammation (chancre), parasites disseminate through the hematolymphatic system, multiply in blood (with cyclic density fluctuation due to variant surface glycoprotein antigenic switching - a repertoire of ~1000 VSGs) and extravascular tissues (skin, muscle, serous membranes, heart). CNS invasion (second stage) follows weeks-to-months (rhodesiense) or months-to-years (gambiense), with predominantly white-matter perivascular astrocyte/microglial proliferation and Mott (morular) cells containing IgM; the cortex and neurons are spared until terminal stages, and inflammatory lesions are largely reversible so neuropsychiatric features may resolve with treatment (p.1789-1790, 1793-1794).
additionalDifferentials: Chagas chronic cardiomyopathy: other dilated cardiomyopathies including ischemic heart disease (advanced Chagas carries a worse prognosis) (p.1790)
Chagas megaesophagus: achalasia and other causes of dysphagia (p.1789)
Chagas megacolon: Hirschsprung's disease and other causes of severe chronic constipation (p.1789)
T. b. gambiense HAT systemic features: hypothyroidism and adrenal insufficiency (but thyroid/adrenal function tests are normal) (p.1794)
HAT neuropsychiatric presentation: primary psychiatric illness (mental disorder is a key HAT feature easily misdiagnosed) (p.1794)
T. b. rhodesiense acute febrile illness: malaria (suspect HAT especially if malaria tests are negative) (p.1794)
infectionMimics: Malaria (acute febrile illness overlapping T. b. rhodesiense HAT; HAT suspected when malaria tests are negative) (p.1794)
Other febrile/systemic infections in returned travelers from endemic areas (p.1794)
nonInfectiousMimics: Hypothyroidism and adrenal insufficiency (HAT systemic features, but endocrine tests normal) (p.1794)
additionalInvestigations: Chagas acute/reactivation: blood microscopy after concentration (Strout method, microhematocrit) or PCR of peripheral blood, CSF, or other body fluids (p.1790)

Chagas chronic: serology for anti-T. cruzi IgG - conventional/recombinant ELISA and immunofluorescence; two positive tests with different techniques/antigens to confirm (third test if discordant); immunochromatographic rapid tests for first-line screening where labs are limited (p.1790)

Chagas congenital: cord/peripheral blood microscopy or PCR in first days/weeks (testing after 4 weeks most accurate; earlier PCR may be falsely positive); serology at 9 months once maternal antibodies cleared (p.1790)

Chagas cardiac staging: 12-lead ECG with 30-s strip; echocardiography and 24-h Holter for chamber dilation, apical aneurysm, ventricular dysfunction, arrhythmias; MRI or electrophysiologic studies as indicated (p.1791)
Chagas digestive staging: barium esophagography and barium enema (first-line); esophageal manometry (p.1791)
Chagas comorbidity workup: screen for other cardiovascular risk factors, immunosuppressive conditions, and other chronic infections (e.g., Strongyloides stercoralis, HIV) (p.1791)
HAT T. b. gambiense screening: card agglutination test for trypanosomiasis (CATT) or lateral flow tests; ELISA/immunofluorescence/indirect hemagglutination in reference labs (p.1795)

HAT confirmation: microscopy of trypanosomes in lymph (cervical lymph node puncture), blood (microhematocrit centrifugation; most sensitive is miniature anion-exchange centrifugation, ~90%), skin biopsy, or CSF; thin/thick Giemsa smears and concentration for T. b. rhodesiense (p.1795)
HAT staging: lumbar puncture with CSF examination (leukocyte count, trypanosomes after centrifugation) (p.1795)
Supportive HAT labs (nonspecific): anemia, thrombocytopenia, elevated C-reactive protein and IgM (p.1794)
redFlags: Chronic Chagas cardiomyopathy with high risk of sudden death - bundle branch block is often the first sign and may be asymptomatic for years before serious conduction disease, arrhythmias, and LV dysfunction; 5-year mortality 2-63% depending on cardiac damage, leading causes cardiac failure and sudden death, then stroke (p.1790)
Chagas digestive determinate disease: dysphagia, regurgitation, severe constipation, fecaloma, volvulus, and toxic colonic dilation (p.1790)
Intramural thrombus or LV apical aneurysm in Chagas cardiomyopathy - risk of cardioembolic stroke (p.1790-1791)

Chagas reactivation in immunosuppression (HIV with CD4 <100/uL, post-transplant, hematologic malignancy): myocarditis, Toxoplasma-like focal brain lesion, meningoencephalitis - AIDS-defining when clinically manifest (p.1789-1790)
Untreated HAT is usually lethal - early diagnosis is crucial; second-stage (CNS) disease with decreased consciousness, dementia, epilepsy progressing to coma and death (p.1794)
T. b. rhodesiense terminal sepsis-like illness with disseminated intravascular coagulation and multi-organ failure, plus more rapid evolution to coma and death than gambiense (p.1794)

Severe second-stage HAT signs warranting non-fexinidazole staging/treatment: mental confusion, abnormal behavior, logorrhea, anxiety, ataxia, tremor, motor weakness, speech impairment, abnormal gait/movements, or seizures (p.1795)
harrison.prognosis: Chagas: 5-10% of acute (early) infections resolve spontaneously without treatment; most become chronic, of whom 60-70% never develop tissue damage (indeterminate form) and 30-40% progress over decades to cardiac, digestive, or mixed disease. Acute-phase mortality is low (0.1-5% with oral transmission or myocarditis/encephalitis). Determinate chronic disease 5-year mortality is 2-63% depending on extent of cardiac damage, with cardiac failure, sudden death, and stroke the leading causes; advanced cardiac damage carries a worse prognosis than other cardiomyopathies. African trypanosomiasis: untreated HAT is usually fatal. With properly followed guidelines, >95% of first- and second-stage T. b. gambiense HAT patients are definitively cured (fexinidazole, pentamidine, nifurtimox-eflornithine), overall case-fatality <1% except in very advanced cases; relapses can occur long after treatment, so follow-up every 6 months for at least 2 years is advised. Second-stage T. b. rhodesiense HAT carries a 5-10% risk of death during/after melarsoprol treatment, though relapses are very rare (p.1790, 1796).
pitfalls: More than 90% of Chagas infections go undiagnosed and are often identified late once chronic complications develop; the majority of infected individuals are asymptomatic (indeterminate form) (p.1790)
International tourists visiting endemic areas are at very low risk of Chagas and travel-related cases are rare - the at-risk group is migrants from endemic regions, not casual travelers (p.1789)
There is no evidence that bedbugs transmit T. cruzi to humans despite laboratory potential (p.1788)
There is no predictor of which chronic-phase Chagas patients will progress to clinical disease (p.1790)

Chronic-phase Chagas PCR has limited sensitivity (50-80%): a negative result cannot be interpreted, so patients with negative PCR but persistent positive serology should still be considered potentially infective (p.1790, 1792)
Early congenital Chagas PCR may be falsely positive (maternal T. cruzi DNA fragments); testing after 4 weeks of age is most accurate (p.1790)

In adults with chronic Chagas cardiomyopathy, benznidazole has no impact on disease progression or mortality, and neither benznidazole nor nifurtimox is effective against digestive complications (KNOWLEDGE only - no dosing) (p.1791-1792)
HAT clinical/biologic features (anemia, thrombocytopenia, raised CRP and IgM) are not specific enough to treat on suspicion - diagnostic confirmation is required in all patients (p.1794)
Absence of fever does not rule out T. b. gambiense HAT (fever is more frequent in travelers than natives) (p.1794)
HAT systemic features may mimic hypothyroidism or adrenal insufficiency but thyroid/adrenal tests are normal; mental disorder may be misdiagnosed as primary psychiatric illness (p.1794)
Trypanids (HAT rashes) are almost impossible to detect on dark skin and have been reported only in Caucasians (p.1794)
HIV co-infection does not appear to increase HAT risk, and the virus's effect on HAT presentation is unknown (p.1794)
Eflornithine is ineffective against T. b. rhodesiense, so melarsoprol remains in use for second-stage rhodesiense disease (KNOWLEDGE only) (p.1796)
harrison.severityClassification: Chagas (T. cruzi infection stages, Table 234-1): Acute phase (including congenital, vector-borne, oral, transfusion, transplant) lasting 2-8 weeks, mostly asymptomatic; Chronic indeterminate form (normal exam and ECG, no attributable mortality, lifelong or until determinate phase); Chronic determinate form (cardiac, digestive, or mixed organ damage years to decades after infection); Acute reactivation in severe immunosuppression. Diagnostic procedure of choice by stage: microscopy after concentration / PCR for acute, early congenital, and reactivation; serology (two positive tests) for chronic indeterminate and determinate. HAT staging: First stage (hemolymphatic, no CNS involvement) vs Second stage (CNS/meningoencephalitic), defined by CSF leukocytes >5/uL and/or trypanosomes; nonsevere second stage = 6-99 leukocytes/uL CSF, severe second stage = >=100 leukocytes/uL CSF (p.1790, 1795).

management: Treat acute, congenital, reactivated or early chronic Chagas disease with the antitrypanosomal drugs benznidazole or nifurtimox
Manage chronic Chagas cardiomyopathy with guideline-directed heart failure therapy, antiarrhythmics, pacing or a defibrillator, and anticoagulation for thromboembolic risk
Treat digestive Chagas (mega-oesophagus and megacolon) with dietary measures, laxatives or prokinetics, and endoscopic or surgical intervention for advanced megaviscera

Treat gambiense human African trypanosomiasis with fexinidazole or, according to stage, pentamidine for early disease and nifurtimox-eflornithine combination therapy for late central nervous system disease
Treat rhodesiense human African trypanosomiasis with suramin for the early haemolymphatic stage and melarsoprol for late-stage central nervous system involvement
Screen for and treat Strongyloides and HIV before immunosuppressive or antitrypanosomal therapy, and monitor for drug toxicity during treatment
Screen at-risk relatives, pregnant women and blood and organ donors, and pursue vector control to prevent transmission
Refer to infectious diseases and organ-specific specialists in cardiology, gastroenterology and neurology according to the manifestations
